acceptedAnswer.text: Cocaine withdrawal is the group of physical and psychological symptoms that appear when a regular cocaine user cuts down or stops. Because the brain relies on cocaine to release dopamine, stopping causes a crash in mood, energy, and motivation, along with strong cravings, until the brain rebalances.

mainEntity.name: How long does cocaine withdrawal last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Acute cocaine withdrawal usually lasts about one to two weeks, with the worst of the crash in the first few days. Lingering low mood, poor sleep, and occasional cravings can continue for several weeks or a few months during post-acute withdrawal.

mainEntity.name: Can you die from cocaine withdrawal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cocaine withdrawal on its own rarely causes death, but severe depression with suicidal thoughts during the crash is a real risk, and relapsing on a drug supply often contaminated with fentanyl carries a high overdose risk.

mainEntity.name: What are the first signs of cocaine withdrawal?

acceptedAnswer.text: The first signs usually appear within a few hours of the last dose and include sudden exhaustion, a heavy low mood, increased appetite, and either deep sleepiness or restless insomnia, with cravings fading briefly before returning.

mainEntity.name: Are there medications for cocaine withdrawal?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no medication approved specifically for cocaine use disorder in Canada or the United States. Doctors may use medications off label for symptoms like insomnia or depression, but the core of treatment is behavioural therapy.

mainEntity.name: Do you need medical detox for cocaine?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not everyone does, but medical detox is strongly recommended for severe use, a history of depression or suicidal thoughts, or heavy polysubstance use, because it keeps you safe during the crash and connects you to ongoing treatment.

mainEntity.name: How long does cocaine stay in your system?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cocaine is usually detectable in blood and saliva for about one to two days, in urine for two to four days with occasional use and up to about two weeks with heavy use, and in hair for around 90 days.

mainEntity.name: What treatment works best for cocaine addiction?

acceptedAnswer.text: The strongest evidence supports behavioural treatments, especially contingency management and cognitive behavioural therapy, often within an inpatient or outpatient program, along with dual diagnosis care for underlying mental health conditions.

faqs.question: What is the cocaine crash?

answer_blocks.text: The crash is the first phase of withdrawal, starting within hours of stopping. It brings intense fatigue, long or disrupted sleep, big appetite, and a flat or depressed mood as the brain’s overstimulated reward system suddenly powers down. It is exhausting but usually short, lasting a few days.

faqs.question: What is post-acute withdrawal syndrome from cocaine?

answer_blocks.text: Post-acute withdrawal syndrome, or PAWS, is a longer phase after acute withdrawal where milder symptoms come and go for weeks or months. People notice waves of low mood, poor sleep, and sudden cravings as the brain slowly heals. It is normal and manageable, not a sign of relapse.

faqs.question: Why is cocaine mixed with fentanyl so dangerous?

answer_blocks.text: Fentanyl is an extremely potent opioid, and even a small amount hidden in cocaine can stop someone’s breathing. Because street cocaine is increasingly contaminated, the overdose risk during a relapse is very high, especially after a period of abstinence when tolerance has dropped. Carrying naloxone is a sensible precaution.

blocks.text: If you have ever tried to stop using cocaine and found yourself flattened by exhaustion, low mood, and cravings so strong they scared you, you already know that withdrawal is real. It rarely looks like the dramatic, sweat-soaked scenes people picture. Cocaine withdrawal is quieter and, in many ways, more insidious. It works on your mind, your sleep, and your sense of hope, and that is exactly why so many people relapse in the first week. Understanding what is coming, and knowing that the worst of it passes, makes a genuine difference.

blocks.text: Quick answer: Cocaine withdrawal is the set of physical and psychological symptoms that appear when a regular user cuts back or stops. Symptoms can begin within a few hours of the last dose and usually include intense fatigue, depressed mood, vivid cravings, increased appetite, and disturbed sleep. Most acute symptoms ease within one to two weeks, though low mood and cravings can linger for months. Cocaine withdrawal is rarely life threatening on its own, but the depression and suicidal thoughts it can trigger make support and monitoring important.

blocks.text: What Is Cocaine Withdrawal?
blocks.html: What Is Cocaine Withdrawal?

blocks.text: Cocaine is a powerful stimulant that floods the brain with dopamine, the chemical tied to pleasure, motivation, and reward. With repeated use, the brain adapts. It produces less dopamine on its own and relies on the drug to feel normal. When the cocaine stops, that borrowed chemistry crashes, and the body and mind have to recalibrate. That recalibration is what we call withdrawal.

blocks.text: Because cocaine is short acting, the comedown often starts quickly, sometimes before the high has fully worn off. This is different from opioids or alcohol, where the physical withdrawal is more visible. With cocaine, the hardest symptoms are emotional and mental, which is one reason people underestimate how difficult stopping can be. blocks.text: Withdrawal Versus a Comedown
blocks.html: Withdrawal Versus a Comedown

blocks.text: People sometimes use “comedown” and “withdrawal” to mean the same thing, but there is a difference. A comedown is the short slump after a single session of use, lasting a day or two. Withdrawal is the longer pattern that shows up in someone who uses regularly and then stops. The comedown is a preview. Withdrawal is the full feature.

blocks.text: Researchers usually describe cocaine withdrawal in three overlapping phases: the crash, acute withdrawal, and a longer extinction phase. The timing varies from person to person depending on how much and how often they used, whether they used powder or crack, their overall health, and whether other substances are involved. The table below gives a realistic map.

blocks.text: The encouraging part is that the sharpest suffering is usually short. The crash is heavy but brief. By the second or third week, most people notice their sleep, appetite, and mood beginning to settle. The cravings that return during the extinction phase are real, but they tend to be shorter and less overwhelming over time, especially with counselling and structure in place. The U.S. National Library of Medicine’s MedlinePlus entry on cocaine withdrawal describes a similar arc.

blocks.text: Why the First Week Is the Riskiest
blocks.html: Why the First Week Is the Riskiest

blocks.text: The days right after stopping are when the crash and the deepest low mood collide. For some people, that low is severe enough to bring on hopelessness or thoughts of suicide, even in those who have never felt that way before. This is a medical reason, not a weakness, and it is the single strongest argument for not going through early cocaine withdrawal completely alone. Having someone check in, or being in a setting where staff can watch for these signs, saves lives.

blocks.text: Post-Acute Withdrawal Syndrome (PAWS)
blocks.html: Post-Acute Withdrawal Syndrome (PAWS)

blocks.text: After the acute phase, some people move into a longer stretch known as post-acute withdrawal syndrome. During PAWS, the brain is still healing its dopamine and reward systems. Symptoms come and go: a few good days, then a wave of low mood, poor sleep, or a sudden craving out of nowhere. PAWS can be discouraging because it feels like backsliding, but it is a normal part of recovery, not a sign of failure. Building a solid relapse prevention plan is the most effective way to ride out these waves without returning to use.

blocks.text: Can You Die From Cocaine Withdrawal?
blocks.html: Can You Die From Cocaine Withdrawal?

blocks.text: Cocaine withdrawal by itself is rarely fatal in the way that severe alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal can be, because it does not usually cause seizures or dangerous swings in blood pressure and heart rhythm during the detox phase. That said, “rarely fatal on its own” is not the same as safe. Two serious risks stand out.

blocks.text: The first is the mental health crisis. Severe depression and suicidal thoughts during the crash are genuine medical emergencies. The second is the danger of the current drug supply. Cocaine in Canada is increasingly contaminated with fentanyl and other synthetic opioids, which means a relapse after a period of abstinence can be deadly. If you or someone you love is in immediate danger, call 911 or reach a crisis line right away, and keep naloxone on hand given how often fentanyl now shows up in the cocaine supply.

blocks.text: Cocaine and the Canadian Overdose Crisis
blocks.html: Cocaine and the Canadian Overdose Crisis

blocks.text: Cocaine is often treated as a “safer” party drug than heroin or fentanyl, but the data tell a harder story. According to the Public Health Agency of Canada, there were 7,146 opioid-related deaths in 2024, about 20 every day, with roughly 74 percent involving fentanyl. Stimulants like cocaine are deeply entangled in that crisis. Health Canada’s analysis of multi-drug toxicity deaths found that in 2023, just under half of accidental opioid toxicity deaths also involved a stimulant such as cocaine or methamphetamine.

blocks.text: Cocaine Detox: What It Involves
blocks.html: Cocaine Detox: What It Involves

blocks.text: Detox is the process of clearing cocaine from the body and getting through the acute withdrawal phase safely. For cocaine, detox is less about managing dangerous physical symptoms and more about keeping the person safe, supported, and stable through the crash and the emotional low that follows.

blocks.text: Medically Supervised Detox
blocks.html: Medically Supervised Detox

blocks.text: In a medically supervised detox, a person stays in a safe setting where nurses and physicians monitor their mental and physical health. They can screen for suicidal thinking, treat sleep problems and agitation, manage any co-occurring conditions, and make sure the person is eating and hydrating. If you want a plain-language walkthrough of the whole experience, our guide to what happens at a drug detox centre covers it step by step, and our overview of detox facilities in Canada explains the different settings available.

blocks.text: Can You Detox From Cocaine at Home?
blocks.html: Can You Detox From Cocaine at Home?

blocks.text: Many people do get through cocaine withdrawal at home, and for someone with a strong support system and no serious mental health history, that can be reasonable. The key safeguards are simple: do not be completely alone during the first week, remove access to the drug, watch closely for signs of severe depression or suicidal thoughts, and have a clear plan to get help fast if things worsen. If there is any history of depression, self-harm, or heavy polysubstance use, a supervised setting is far safer. When in doubt, a quick professional assessment can help you choose the right level of care.

blocks.text: Treatment for Cocaine Use Disorder
blocks.html: Treatment for Cocaine Use Disorder

blocks.text: Here is the part that matters most. Getting through withdrawal is only the beginning. Detox clears the drug, but it does not treat the addiction. Without follow-up care, relapse rates are high, which is why the strongest outcomes come from pairing detox with ongoing treatment.

blocks.text: One important fact shapes cocaine treatment. Unlike opioid addiction, where medications like methadone and buprenorphine are proven tools, there is no medication approved in Canada or the United States specifically to treat cocaine use disorder. Researchers have studied drugs such as modafinil, topiramate, disulfiram, and bupropion, and doctors sometimes use medications off label to ease specific symptoms like insomnia or depression, but the backbone of cocaine treatment is behavioural, not pharmaceutical.

blocks.text: If you are the person watching a loved one go through this, your role matters more than you might think. Practical, non-judgmental support goes a long way: keeping the environment calm, making sure they eat and rest, and gently encouraging professional help rather than lecturing.

blocks.text: Frequently Asked Questions About Cocaine Withdrawal
blocks.html: Frequently Asked Questions About Cocaine Withdrawal

blocks.text: What is cocaine withdrawal?
blocks.html: What is cocaine withdrawal?

blocks.text: Cocaine withdrawal is the group of physical and psychological symptoms that appear when a regular cocaine user cuts down or stops. Because the brain has come to rely on cocaine to release dopamine, stopping causes a crash in mood, energy, and motivation, along with strong cravings, until the brain rebalances.

blocks.text: How long does cocaine withdrawal last?
blocks.html: How long does cocaine withdrawal last?

blocks.text: Acute cocaine withdrawal usually lasts about one to two weeks, with the worst of the crash in the first few days. Lingering symptoms like low mood, poor sleep, and occasional cravings can continue for several weeks or a few months as the brain heals, a stage known as post-acute withdrawal.

blocks.text: What are the first signs of cocaine withdrawal?
blocks.html: What are the first signs of cocaine withdrawal?

blocks.text: The first signs usually appear within a few hours of the last dose and include sudden exhaustion, a heavy low mood, increased appetite, and either deep sleepiness or restless insomnia. Cravings often fade briefly during this crash before returning strongly in the following days.

The real dangers are severe depression with suicidal thoughts during the crash, and the high overdose risk of relapsing on a drug supply now often contaminated with fentanyl.

It is exhausting but usually short, lasting a few days.

blocks.text: The Bottom Line
blocks.html: The Bottom Line

blocks.text: Cocaine withdrawal is hard, but it is survivable, and it is temporary. The crash feels like the floor has dropped out, yet within a couple of weeks most people find their sleep, appetite, and mood beginning to return. The bigger challenge is what comes after, when cravings resurface and old triggers pull at you. That is where real treatment, whether a structured treatment program, counselling, or a supportive community, turns a white-knuckle detox into lasting recovery.
